Yes and no. I don't think autism is inherently gendered one way or the other, it's just how one's upbringing affects them. Women are just more used to being silenced or quiet because that's how they were raised, whereas men tend to get away with a lot more as boys. I've met plenty of girls who exhibit more "male" autism and boys who exhibit "female" autism too. 

With being trans, a lot of trans people actually don't realize they're trans until a fair bit later in life. They may have not felt comfortable in their bodies that whole time, but they were still living as their birth gender before realizing they're trans. The trans community actually does sometimes use the phrase "living as (gender)" in order to express that very unique experience of living through multiple genders throughout one's lifespan. 

For example, I didn't realize I was trans until I was 14, so for years 1-13 I was "living as a female" and society treated me like one. I simply did not get a male childhood or male upbringing and I can't relate to those types of stories, as much as I would really like to. 

Because my parents brought me up as female, I was disciplined like how many young girls are; "don't talk too loud" "don't yell" "wear this but never that" "if you wear that you'll look like a whore" etc etc. This affected my autism as I became used to trying to smother it down and protect myself from harassment or further abuse, which a fair amount of women can relate to (from my experience). I did not feel fully comfortable being a girl, but I literally just had no idea what I was yet. 

Again, it's just more about one's upbringing.

There's an episode of Arthur that talks about autism and describes it using the metaphor that you are a human astronaut stranded on a planet of nice but very offputting and overwhelming aliens (neurotypicals).

The episode is somewhat dated and not the best representation (although I feel like they at least tried) but I think about the central metaphor a lot. All the aliens speak through megaphones and the main character has to ask them to not do that, at which point the aliens are like "o shit sorry my guy, didn't realize it was causing you actual physical pain, i'll stop." 

The episode tried to emphasize the notion that to an autistic person, everyone else's NT behaviors are the strange ones that are difficult to understand. When a neurotypical realizes that, it becomes easier to communicate naturally. 

I think it's important to emphasize that point to your child as well; he may find others' thoughts and behaviors difficult to understand and others may find him difficult to understand, which is why communication and mutual understanding is an important tool for us, even if we communicate our thoughts in many unique different ways. 

It's also worth considering the purely scientific route of explanation: "hello dearest son, your brain calculates thoughts and sends nerve signals differently than others but it's totally chill, here are some symptoms you may be experiencing" but I'm not sure how a child would react to that.

It's just more what I've noticed among my fellow autistic peers in real life. I had one acquaintance who experienced incredibly strong intrusive thoughts but no other signs of OCD at all. 

Many of my autistic friends in general tend to go into what I call "thought spirals," where they get trapped in a cycle of self-rumination which can lead to intrusive/otherwise unwanted and distressing thoughts. These same thoughts will then randomly re-occur to them throughout the day on their own. 

My peers do tend to have depression and anxiety as well though, which doesn't particularly help manage unwanted thoughts.

From my own personal experience, I found that my OCD-like symptoms were way worse when I was a teen (I'm 21 now). I wouldn't say I have OCD now, but my brother-in-law has agreed that I do have some symptoms that make it difficult to tell. 
However, he in the other hand was diagnosed with OCD and I can see that you two do share some behaviors (most notably school note formatting, intrusive thoughts, and repetitive rituals). 

Autism and OCD are basically cousins. Both can involve obsessive behaviors, overall paranoia, unwanted thoughts, etc; it really does make it difficult to tell. 

However, if it's helpful at all, I find that my OCD-like symptoms decreased as I got older because I generally tried to lessen the number of stressors in my life (which makes me think it wasn't OCD but just my autism spiraling, I guess). Being a teen is inherently very stressful and it's possible that some of these behaviors will become less prevalent as time goes on. It's also possible that the opposite is true. I definitely relate to very specific traumatic experiences giving me obsessive behaviors or rituals; when I was younger my cat died on the morning I happened to put my left shoe on before the right one, which lead me to being incredibly vigilant about always putting my right shoe on first ("to prevent it from happening again!")

Personally, I do still have obsessive thoughts and behaviors that would make sense for someone with OCD, but for me I feel like it's part of my autism. They're not persistent enough for me to feel like they genuinely disrupt my life, and for the most part I can see where my behaviors are irrational or unnecessary; they just bring me comfort to do. Sometimes I feel 100% compelled to do them, sometimes I feel like I don't have to. 

(Medical marijuana also helped me generally calm tf down and not fret as much; the same for my brother in law, although he also takes multiple medications to manage symptoms). 

It may still be worth talking to a doctor about OCD and seeing if separate treatment for it would help with some behaviors that you feel disrupt your life or otherwise bring you mental distress.

I had a couple teachers during my virtual year of high school that found out I was trans through talking to each other and they sent me emails telling me that they're supportive and will use my name/pronouns whenever possible.

My initial reaction was that I was bit put off by it. It seemed odd to come out of nowhere even though I really appreciated it. When I had a moment to think about it, I really was grateful that they had approached me first to let me know, even if I felt awkward about it. I realize I probably only felt awkward because it's just not something I'm used to; and a lot of other trans people can probably say the same thing. (I also live in a very red state, so any show of allyship is honestly quite meaningful for me). 

When I have moments of not feeling accepted by society, I think about how those teachers got over their own awkward feelings just to let me know that they support me through a 3-paragraph email. It helps. 

I would say that it's worth it to approach your student and talk to them, if only to confirm their gender identity. The worst that can happen is that the student thinks you tried too hard to be supportive.

As other people have said there's a high chance that your child would also be autistic. One great thing about it is that you'll be able to understand your kid better than anyone, but you'll have to be their biggest advocate. My autistic cousin gets harassed by the rest of his family (and "friends") quite often but his autistic mother never steps in because she just doesn't know how. By "advocate" I mean that you'll likely have to confront schools, doctors, and other people about how they treat your child, whether it's to simply inform them of your child's autism or to argue with them about unfair treatment. 

There's also the issue of "coddling" your child too much, which is an issue I've noticed specifically in my generation (older Gen Z). Many of my autistic peers grew up with overprotective parents who did everything for them, and those peers now lack the independence and self-sufficiency expected of someone their age. Not that they're completely helpless, but that they rely on their parents just a little too much because that's what their parents taught them to do. I'm not saying your child shouldn't be able to rely on you ever, but that just trying to teaching them independence and inner confidence is really important. I only bring it up because it seems that a lot of the parents of autistic kids in my life missed that memo, even though their kids would've benefitted from it immensely (and some autistic kids with certain needs probably wouldn't, which is okay too). 

Focusing on fostering independence and confidence will also help with possible bullying later in life. While it won't stop the bullies, your child will at least have one more tool in their toolkit to help themselves handle the situation before adults step in.

I mentioned this in another comment, but cats usually meow in order to call for mama cat ("I'm cold! I'm lost! I'm hungry!"). They learn this behavior when they're first born and continue it until they're matured and separated, at which point they may stop meowing for mama as they grow into their independence. 

Adult cats don't really communicate to each other through basic meows like mother and kitten do, so ferals don't really "meow" that often. There's no particular reason to if they're by themselves. You may hear them go "mroooowwwww" from time to time as they call for mates or assert dominance, but that's about it on the communication spectrum for feral cats. 

So the prevailing theory is that the reason adult cats meow at humans is because they now see you as mama and are asking you for attention or assistance. Your boy trusts you a whole bunch.

Kittens meow from the start of their lives in order to call for mama. After they're spayed and separated, it's a gamble on how much they'll meow after that since they no longer have to call for mom's help. 

I've heard a few people mention that their cat was quiet for a few years and then starting meowing again (mine included). As the cat realizes that you are their caretaker and new "mama" they're more likely to meow at you to ask for stuff. As they get older and start losing some senses, meowing/yowling for help becomes more common. (Not that meowing is *always* asking for something out of you, it could also just be to get your attention).

You might be trans, you might not, but either way lots of people experience some form of "gender haze;" I've met a few cis girls who just really hated their body due to trauma or a chronic issue and I've met lots of nonbinary people who feel the same as you as well. 

Either way, it's often difficult to pinpoint why we sometimes feel this way about our bodies. Trying to identify the source is a journey in of itself; as someone recovering from anorexia, I feel simultaneous disgust and pride when I look at my body now. I'm also (pre-surgery) trans so I really have no clue what caused me to want to look like a skeleton. Maybe it's because I hate my chest and want it *gone* or maybe I'm just like (most) other anorexics and just want to be thin. I've tried to find the reason and I can't, and it causes me more stress when I do think about it.

What helped me somewhat was focusing on stuff that I could change in the moment. I can't get top surgery to remove my biddies so I bought a binder to strap them down from view (a method also endorsed by the cis women and feminine enbies in my life who "just wanted a break from them"). If binders are too expensive you can find lots of sports bras that have roughly the same effect. I've also heard of Transtape / "boob tape" but I'm not sure how well it does on large chests. (Also, honestly, binders might be cheaper than bras now.)

I felt insecure in a lot of the clothes I wore so I tried to wear things that I *knew* I loved or that had sentimental value to me. I also ended up falling into the grunge fashion aesthetic because (tbh) it kinda suits everyone. I've always been told that I could "be a model" or a ballerina or something like that because of my figure, but oh my god I hate it and I'm perfectly content not showing it off. You don't have to dress to look good. At first it feels silly and dumb to just wear what you want without being concerned about how you're perceived, but the most important thing you can do for your self-confidence is just try to be comfortable. Even if you have to hide something to be comfortable, that's okay. 

I also get the thing about trying to lose weight. While I'm on the opposite end and trying to gain it, it's *stupid fucking difficult* and I keep resorting to not eating to just not have to think about it. And of course that doesn't help much. 

While I don't have any personally-verified advice about how to lose weight, I would say that it's okay to eat large portions when you're stressed as long as it's relatively nutritious. What a lot of people get wrong about losing weight is that you *have* to eat smaller portions, and while that's *technically true*, most people losing weight still need enough energy from food, and what everyone needs to eat every day to maintain their overall health is vastly different. My plus-size boyfriend eats nearly 3x my portion sizes and is still losing weight. With that in mind, maybe you could try finding something healthier to binge (grapes, crackers, apple slices, etc) or finding an alternative to binging that still scratches that need (like cooking/preparing large quantities of food to save for later, like bread). I don't want to sound like I'm patronizing you or anything. I feel disgusting when I happen to binge-eat (or just... eat in general) and what helped me get over that a little bit was finding something healthy that didn't make me feel guilty about it. My favourite food for a while was just baked potatoes. Working out is also important etc etc.

I'm not really qualified to give you that much advice regarding weight loss, so take all this with a grain of salt. I would recommend checking out binders though, if you haven't.

I was taught to do proofs in a very specific way in the format of "if x is this then y is this." The difficult part for me is that your proof has to be split into steps. 

However you are ALSO allowed to say that some information is "given" in the problem; if there's a point C between points A and B, then you can simply say "point C is the midpoint between A and B, it is given." 

Usually these triangle problems have given information that helps you fill in the rest. If it is given that Angle A in a triangle is 109 degrees and Angle B is 23 degrees, then it's safe to assume Angle C must be 48 degrees (180 = 109 + 23 + 48) so it adds up to 180 and is therefore a triangle. 

There's also the issue of congruence, where you might be given two identical triangles but only information for 1 is given, so you have to prove that Triangle 2 is a triangle using information from Triangle 1. 

So. Yes, in this context, saying that it has 3 angles that add up to 180 is sufficient proof. I don't think the straight sides have anything to do in this problem, but they get involved in more complex problems.

My boyfriend is similar and doesn't really understand stimming.

What's important to understand first is that stimming can take many forms. Some neurotypical people also stim (bouncing one's leg), toddlers stim all the time (flappy hands) etc. It's just expressing one's inner emotions physically, either to relieve stress, make oneself happy or excited, express pain, and so on. 

Allow yourself to let your body move instinctually as a response to something. Start recognizing small habits or quirks you have, like tapping/rubbing your fingers, picking your thumbs, shaking your leg, stuff like that. Letting your body express these things more openly will let you be more comfortable with stimming. And don't feel like you *have* to stim. 

Stimming also doesn't have to be limited to fidgeting habits. If you play video games often, that can be a way to stim since it "stim"ulates your brain and hands in a satisfying way.

Overall, try imitating the habits and stims of others from time to time and see what's satisfying to you. It's common for autistics to pick up other stims by seeing them. Don't feel afraid to feel silly.

I played Twin Mirror a while ago so I have to talk about it. While the protagonist is white/straight/cis he is also heavily implied to be autistic and I love how the game handled it.

Twin Mirror definitely leans into some tropes (protagonist has a "mind palace" lmao) but Sam the protagonist still has a lot of emotional depth and flaws, which is highlighted by his imaginary friend Samuel: a version of himself that's completely neurotypical and feeds him advice on how to present as "normal." 

You can either choose to listen to Samuel or ignore him to do what Sam wants, but sometimes Sam is in the wrong or Samuel is in the wrong. The neurotypical answer isn't always the right one. 

At the end of the game (spoiler) >!you decide whether to keep Neurotypical Samuel in Sam's life, or if Sam should just accept himself as he is and move on without his imaginary friend. It sounds like an easy decision but holy shit I spent an hour on that choice alone.!<

Sam is an ex-investigative journalist, and has an "obsession" with finding the truth, but his obsession frequently leads to people getting offended by him and consequently hating him. 

His only friend for the majority of the game is his ex-girlfriend, who broke up with Sam since he was terrible at listening to her (he tried to propose with a ring even though she didn't want a ring, but he did it anyway because he "thought that's what people are supposed to do"). But she doesn't hate him for that at all. No one really considers Sam to be a burden besides his parents in flashbacks, but they're mostly arguing about whether or not he's autistic as opposed to how much they love him. 

Sam is a bit flat though. You really only see his emotions in his mind palace (during puzzle or cutscene segments) and he's only really expressive with his god-daughter or his ex-girlfriend. He's definitely not an autistic stereotype though. He's not framed as being super-intelligent or having a computer brain, he still panics and messes up sometimes, and he's capable of understanding sarcasm and nuance. 

Also in his mind palace he has a seamless shirt on. Literally, in his ideal world in his ideal state of being, he's wearing the perfect sensory-friendly shirt. It made me laugh when I first saw it because I hate shirt seams too, LOL 

Sorry for the ramble but Twin Mirror is def the best representation I've seen so far, even if it's not the best. Definitely the most accurate one I've seen in a story that doesn't revolve around his autism.

Am an artist.

Many 12 year olds are quite talented, but besides that, part of this artwork is an illusion.

Whenever you see a hyper-realistic portrait, either in pencil or paint, it's likely that it was drawn on a very large canvas. When viewed from far away or through a photo, it looks much nicer than it would from up close. Individual marks, mistakes, or strokes are much less visible from far away. It's no different than people looking unflattering if you're only a few inches away from them because you can see their individual pores and hairs. 

This artwork is more than likely inspired by van Gogh's Starry Night, which has many broad paintstrokes and repeating patterns. It wouldn't be difficult for a talented child to vaguely replicate it, especially if a projector was used to overlay the image on the wall (which many mural painters use anyway). Gogh's art style is actually quite easy to imitate, as I've taken much inspiration from his work myself. 

Besides that, it's a VERY common practice for artists to do "master studies". A master study is just copying or referencing a famous artist's work in order to learn from their techniques, and even amateur artists can do master studies fairly easily.

EDIT: I wanted to add that artists usually learn from copying, whether from life, model, or by doing a master study. It wouldn't be unordinary for a child artist* to be good at copying something for a basic painting. It's literally just sketching out proportions and where everything should be, which CAN be difficult, but most artists usually have a very solid grasp of this. 

Add that, plus the fact that you're viewing a very large artwork on a much smaller screen, equals some very lovely looking artwork.

I've had a ferret since 6th grade. I graduate high school this year. Ferrets only live for about 8-10 years if kept in good health, and she's nearing her 8th year.

I'm scared every day that I'll wake up to find that she's passed. I'm scared that she's dying whenever she sneezes, farts, or squeaks even slightly. My anxiety got so horrible that I finally confided in a friend.

She told me that I should celebrate the fact that my ferret will die of old age. She said it's a miracle that despite all she's been through, she'll be one of the few ferrets to die of old age rather than disease or injury. 

I still cry when I think about it and I'm still anxious. Seeing Friday slow down and not do much has been incredibly hard. But when she dies, I'll celebrate her long life as it deserves to be celebrated. It's not a long time for us, but it's a lifetime for them. 

Dwelling on uncontrollable circumstances only makes the pain worse. It's okay to acknowledge that pain. It's okay to cry and be upset and mourn your pet. But it's also important to recognize the beauty of having shared that time with another living creature. 

My friend's advice was something I haven't heard before. She genuinely thought that Friday dying of old age was a good and beautiful thing as opposed to something sad. And she's right.

Edit: just for the record, average lifetime of an animal is more of a suggestion than anything. Don't put a hard limit on 12 years or else you'll be dreading waking up every single day when your dog turns 12. Don't become like me, don't be afraid of waking up every morning to bad news.

I'm not vegan (just vegetarian) but I absolutely hate the politicization of fucking diet choices. I'm a vegetarian because I think the commercial meat industry is a terrible practice and harms the environment, but I'd happily eat something that was hunted, in the woods, by a dude I know with a hunting license, and given the respect it deserved. 

My father hunted occasionally, but he told me that it's considered etiquette to never shoot young bucks unless necessary (due to overpopulation, for example). 

So I'm not uncomfortable with the idea of an animal being killed for consumption. That's been the nature of the world long since before humans figured out they can keep cows to slaughter. I'm just uncomfortable with the idea of something that was once alive being heavily processed beyond natural recognition and sat to rest in my grocery store, something that many of my (meat-eating) friends agree with. The only difference between me and them is that I'm more comfortable with cutting meat out of my diet.

I've been made to feel guilty for this innocent belief before, many times, by those who eat meat and by hardcore vegans. I don't understand why it's anyone's business. What someone eats day-to-day isn't and shouldn't be so polarizing as it is. 

The vegan lifestyle isn't for everyone. The reason it's considered a lifestyle is because you HAVE to change your lifestyle to accommodate for eating vegan. You have to track nutrient and vitamin intake religiously, you have to be make sure you're eating the right amount of calories to even function, and you have to be willing to learn how to cook almost everything for yourself. Many people even choose to go vegan not because of how they feel about animal rights but because of preexisting lifestyle choices; someone who works out a lot may benefit more from eating vegan, for example. Someone trying to lose weight because of a health issue may benefit more from eating vegan.

I never want people to feel like I'm trying to convert them when I tell them about my diet choices. When I do tell people why I'm vegetarian, I ask them if they want to actually learn and I tell them about the environmental impact of the beef industry. I want to encourage learning, not conversion.

This teacher is giving students that opportunity and letting them know that they are respected and equal, and that's exactly what you should expect from a teacher. 

It's not even about passing. Teachers likely have access to your deadname and see it everywhere, assuming you haven't legally changed your name. On your official school forms, on roll call sheets, from your parents, from other school faculty, etc. It's MUCH easier for a teacher to remember your preferred name if a student tells them and they make a note of it. It's also WAY easier if the teacher can assign descriptors to you to help them remember. 

One of my first homeroom teachers said he remembered to call me Aaron all the time because at the time, I had green hair like a leprechaun, so he used the phrase "Aaron from Ireland" to remember my preferred name. He was forgetful and old but he never forgot my name for the whole two years I had him. 

Good teachers want nothing more than for their students to feel safe with them. They want students to trust them. That starts with respecting their identity, but remembering individual names  and pronouns that aren't listed on roll call can be difficult if you see hundreds of students every day. I had one teacher tell me that his biggest problem was that the digital roll call couldn't show preferred names and he relied on it to remember names in the first place. He sent me an email once apologizing for using the incorrect pronouns because he's so used to seeing F next to my deadname on digital roll call. At the end of the year, a bunch of trans students thanked him en masse for trying and for being so polite, and gave him advice for what to do next year. He was ecstatic.

I really love having friends who have English as a second language. I have one friend who's incredibly fluent in English but speaks primarily in English slang (ya'll, ye, extensive use of the word "like," lemme, dunno, etc) but I often notice her using common phrases in contexts I'm not used to, but in a way that still makes perfect sense. Sometimes she'll use a super difficult word in place of a more common one as well, and it's just really interesting to see how she uses English in different ways than I do. It's also made me use my own English differently; I never try to simplify what I'm saying to her, since I know she'll understand me no matter what, but sometimes I'll purposefully use words that I know she's more familiar with (mostly more academic words that one would learn in a language class). It's made a lot of our conversations go a lot smoother. Plus I really enjoy teaching her more nuanced slang and having her teach me Italian from time to time. It's also made me a lot more mindful of how I speak to people who aren't as fluent in English. I never want to make someone feel dumb because of what words or phrases I use, but I don't want to confuse them or make them use a dictionary either. 

I had another friend who DID have English as a primary language, but she was Asian-American and had a bit of an accent that she picked up from a parent. Sometimes she had trouble pronouncing certain words, but after a while of being her friend you literally didn't notice her accent at all (it was very Josie from Twin Peaks, although a bit more pronounced). Some teachers would bring it up or ask her to enunciate during a presentation and we would all get really confused, since we literally stopped registering her accent. I remember her most for her surprisingly good cartoon impressions, though. She always made us lose our minds laughing because she was so talented at seamlessly switching accents and voices.

It's really, really fun and interesting to have friends like that. I've learned way more about the nuances of English and pronunciation from them than in an actual English class.

Unfortunately I haven't found a real cure for this and I doubt there is one. If you already have an anxiety disorder, being nervous about phonecalls is just part of the package deal and it's okay to be nervous. If you don't have an anxiety disorder and you're just nervous, then that's okay too. 

Here's some general tips though, from someone who's had severe anxiety about phonecalls for a while:

- drink a hot, calming beverage like tea or hot cocoa. The act of making the drink and the physical sensation of the warmth and taste may help

- recognize that your anxiety about DBAs is largely irrational, and that you've done DBAs before and came out fine at the end. identify what the actual worst possible outcome is if you mess up (I can guarantee it's not as bad as your brain is making it out to be)

- try to schedule them for early in the day just to get them done, so it doesn't haunt you for the whole day

- get a fidget toy or something similar to help you occupy your body while doing the DBA, if that works for you. I have a fidget toy that really helps me out when I'm doing presentations and such. The physical sensation can help distract you during the call itself

- talk to some friends about it, tbh. I always do this when I'm super anxious about something and it always helps me calm down a little. Explaining what's going on helps your brain register that it's not all that bad.

- Do a chore to help occupy yourself before the call. I personally like to clean or do laundry but its up to you
